演奏者以濕潤手指觸碰玻璃碗口，靠摩擦發聲；富蘭克林式將玻璃碗橫置於鐵軸，以腳踏板: The player touches the rims of the glass bowls with wet fingers and the sound comes from friction; in Franklin's version the bowls lie horizontally on an iron spindle turned by a foot pedal, and the pitch is read from the colour painted on the rim. For a start, keep the fingers wet, touch the rim lightly, and control the volume and the length of the note by how hard you press; a little chalk powder can be used if needed to help the sound start.
玻璃琴以濕指摩擦玻璃碗或酒杯發聲，此現象在文藝復興時期已有記載。1740年代Ri: The glass harmonica sounds by rubbing wet fingers on glass bowls or wine glasses, a phenomenon already recorded in the Renaissance. In the 1740s Richard Pockrich played on wine glasses filled with water in London; Edward Delaval improved its tuning and its playability. Benjamin Franklin, inspired by Delaval in 1761, worked with Charles James to build the armonica, with 37 glass bowls turned by a pedal, and Marianne Davies gave the first performance in 1762. After that European monarchs and composers used it; it declined around 1830 and has been revived since the 1980s.
玻璃琴以濕潤手指摩擦依大小排列的玻璃碗或高腳杯邊緣發聲，音色空靈、縈迴，近似長笛: The glass harmonica sounds when wet fingers rub the rims of glass bowls or wine glasses arranged by size; its tone is ethereal and lingering, close to the flute, and long notes can be sustained. Franklin's version has thirty-seven horizontal glass bowls turned by a pedal, the rims painted with colours according to pitch; the pressure of the fingers controls the rise and fall of the volume, and ten bowls can be touched at once. This is different from musical glasses, where upright wine glasses are tuned with water and more than one note at a time is hard to obtain, since the bowls need no retuning once tuned.
玻璃琴是一種以一系列玻璃碗或高腳杯發聲的摩擦體鳴樂器，也屬水晶琴類，Hornbo: The glass harmonica is a friction idiophone sounded by a series of glass bowls or wine glasses, and also belongs among crystal instruments, Hornbostel–Sachs number 133.2. Benjamin Franklin invented the mechanical version in 1761, mounting the glass bowls horizontally on an iron spindle turned by a foot pedal, the player touching the rims with wetted fingers; the rims are painted by pitch and several bowls can be touched at once. European monarchs played it and composers wrote for it.

The glass harmonica is a friction idiophone sounded by a series of glass bowls or wine glasses, and also belongs among crystal instruments, Hornbostel–Sachs number 133.2. Benjamin Franklin invented the mechanical version in 1761, mounting the glass bowls horizontally on an iron spindle turned by a foot pedal, the player touching the rims with wetted fingers; the rims are painted by pitch and several bowls can be touched at once. European monarchs played it and composers wrote for it, and it appears in opera, ballet and public performance.
玻璃琴的發聲體為一系列大小遞減的玻璃碗或高腳杯，以濕潤手指摩擦邊緣發音。富蘭克林: The sounding body of the glass harmonica is a series of glass bowls or wine glasses decreasing in size, sounded by rubbing the rims with wet fingers. Franklin's mechanical version fixes thirty-seven glass bowls horizontally on an iron spindle turned by a foot pedal; the rims are painted in different colours according to pitch, and the fingers are dipped in water when playing and may also be given a little chalk powder. As for the materials of the frame, the stand, the pedal and the other parts, the source does not state them.

聆聽示範可從莫札特K.617、K.356，貝多芬1814年配樂劇《Leonore: For the listening demonstration, start with Mozart's K.617 and K.356, Beethoven's 1814 incidental music for Leonore Prohaska, the aria from Donizetti's opera Il castello di Kenilworth, and the seventh and fourteenth movements of Saint-Saëns's The Carnival of the Animals. Golenthal's 1997 ballet Othello also uses the glass harmonica. After its revival in the 1980s it has appeared in solo, chamber, opera, electronic and popular music.
